label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Nana,

I wish I were sitting in the kitchen with you tonight. I wish I could make the tea, pull up a chair, and tell you all of this myself. Instead, Aunt Denise has agreed to read it to you, which is very good of her. Denise, please try to make me sound composed and emotionally well-adjusted. You have some room to improve on the original.

I’ve been trying to write this all week. I keep starting, getting a few lines down, and closing the laptop. There’s a lot I want to say, and apparently being able to keep computer systems running does not qualify a person to write a letter to their nana.

First, I’m sorry I can’t be there tomorrow. I’m primary on call all week, and I couldn’t find anyone to swap with me. I know you know that. I know you’re not sitting there keeping track of who showed up and who didn’t. But I wanted to be there to carry things and make tea and be useful, and it’s hard being in Toronto while such a big day is happening up there.

I won’t spend the whole letter apologizing, though. You’d get fed up with that pretty quickly, and you’d be right. I love you. I wish I were there. I’ll be there on the December 5 weekend, once this rotation is done. That’s the part to remember.

Fifty-one years on Kathleen Street. I keep thinking about that number. I’m thirty-four, so I’ve never known a version of our family that didn’t have you in that house. It was always there, and you were always there, and when I was little I don’t think it occurred to me that either of those things could ever change.

When I think about the house, I mostly think about the kitchen. I’m sure there were perfectly good other rooms, but the kitchen seems to have collected most of my memories.

I think about staying with you in the summers, watching the Expos or the Jays on that little television while I dried the dishes. I thought I was getting away with something because you let me stay up late. Looking back, you were getting the dishes dried by a child who believed this was a special privilege. Very well played.

I can still remember wanting the game to last longer because then I could stay there longer. There was no big occasion. We were just watching baseball and doing the dishes. I couldn’t have told you then how much I loved it.

And I think about the back steps, early in the morning. You with your tea at six, and me coming out to sit with you. You wouldn’t talk until the cup was done. I didn’t always have the sense to appreciate that arrangement as a kid, but I certainly do now. A quiet cup of tea before anyone starts asking questions seems like an excellent household policy.

I liked sitting beside you. I liked that I didn’t need to have anything to say.

You raised half the family in that kitchen. I wonder whether you realize how much of what we remember happened while you were probably just trying to get through an ordinary day. There would have been dishes to do, food to make, people coming in and out, somebody needing something. Meanwhile, I was having a childhood I still want to go back and visit.

Thank you for all of it. For letting me stay. For feeding me. For finding room for me in your days. For making it feel so easy to be there, even though I know now that looking after people takes work.

Thank you also for teaching me crib at seven and then refusing, on principle, to let me win.

Some grandmothers might have given a small child a little encouragement. You apparently felt that learning to lose properly was encouragement enough. I spent years trying to beat you, and I knew that whenever I finally did, it would count.

I was fifteen the first time I skunked you. You made me a whole pan of butter tarts. I still think that was an extraordinarily gracious response to what must have been a devastating sporting defeat.

I’ve asked for the crib board because I want to keep playing on that one. When I pick it up, I’ll think about sitting across from you, trying to work out whether I’d counted everything, and knowing you absolutely had.

But don’t take this as advance notice that I expect to inherit your position as the family’s best player. I assume you’ll be defending that title for some time yet.

There are things you’ve done for me that probably seemed small to you, but they’ve stayed with me. When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me twenty dollars taped inside a card and wrote, “For pizza, you look thin on the computer.”

I loved that. I was starting this grown-up job in a big city, and you were looking at the screen thinking someone needed to get me supper. You’ve never been especially impressed by distance when there’s a possibility that one of us hasn’t eaten enough.

And last Christmas, when my pager went off during dinner, you asked whether the internet was broken again and whether I’d fixed it. Now every time we talk, you ask, “Did anything break?”

That is a surprisingly accurate summary of my work. People in Toronto use a lot more words to ask essentially the same question.

I like that you ask. I like getting to tell you about my day, even when the answer is mostly that something broke, we fixed it, and then something else had a go.

I’m going to miss the house. I know you will too, even if you’re also looking forward to Elmwood Terrace. Both make sense to me. Fifty-one years is a long time, and there’s so much there to say goodbye to.

I’ve been thinking about Grandpa Walt, too. I wish he were here for this part. I imagine there will be moments tomorrow when missing him feels especially sharp, and I wish I could be beside you for those.

I’m glad Denise is there tonight. I’m glad you get this last evening in the kitchen without having to hurry straight past it.

But I don’t want this letter to turn into a speech where we all get so sad about Kathleen Street that we forget you’ve found a place you actually want to go.

Elmwood looks nice, Nana. I’m looking forward to seeing your room on the second floor, and the big maple outside your window. I’ll even admire the parking lot, although I expect the maple will be doing most of the work for the view.

And a crib league! That seems almost suspiciously well suited to you. I hope they understand that being the new person does not mean you’ll go easy on them. The church ladies could provide references.

I’m proud of you for making this decision yourself. You looked at what you wanted, you picked the place, and you’re doing it. Nobody made you. I know that doesn’t mean every part is easy. Choosing something can be right and still take a lot of courage.

You’re allowed to be excited. I hope you are. I want to hear about the people you meet, what the food’s like, and whether the crib league is up to standard. You’ll have plenty to tell me when I call.

Denise will have the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest. I’ll have the crib board. I’m glad those things will stay with us, because they’re familiar and we love them. But I’m especially glad that on December 5, I’m coming up to see you.

You don’t have to make the new room feel exactly like Kathleen Street for me. I just want to sit down with you, have a proper visit, and find out how you’re settling in.

For tonight, I hope you and Denise have a good cup of tea in that kitchen. Have a cry if you feel like it. Have a laugh, too. There’s been plenty of both in there over the years. I wish I could add my chair to the table, but please know how much I’m thinking about you.

Thank you for giving me so many ordinary, lovely days in that house. I remember them. I’m so grateful I got to be your grandkid in that kitchen.

I love you, Nana. I’ll see you the weekend of December 5. We’ll get the crib board out and have our first game at Elmwood.

And you still don’t have to let me win.
